subject: Careers
scope: Autumn 1 · Weeks 1–7 · Identity & Belonging — Knowing myself
intro: Seven original 40-minute lessons adapted from the supplied Careers slides, pathway pupil resources, teacher resources and Build_Grow_Careers_SoW_2026-27.xlsx. Each pathway follows its own weekly outcomes. Profiles are provisional and reviewed as experience grows. Pupils may use the named fictional cases throughout; label these as case analysis rather than personal employment evidence. These classroom materials do not award a qualification or establish whole-school careers-guidance compliance.

sources.title: Uploaded Careers scheme and lesson resources
sources.note: Build_Grow_Careers_SoW_2026-27.xlsx, BUILD Careers sheet, Autumn 1 rows; Careers_Lesson_1–7_Build_Grow.pptx and matching pupil/teacher DOCX. The supplied Compliance Map is contextual planning, not verified evidence that a benchmark or statutory duty is met.

sources.title: National Careers Service — Explore careers
sources.note: Checked 7 September 2026. Optional teacher-supported follow-up for current role tasks, skills and routes; no live browsing is required for these lessons.

sources.title: National Careers Service — Discover your skills and careers
sources.note: Checked 7 September 2026. Career suggestions are starting points to compare, not a prediction or instruction. No pupil account, questionnaire or personal disclosure is required in this pack.

sources.title: National Careers Service — Understand and develop your skills
sources.note: Checked 7 September 2026. Supports the general ideas of transferable skills, identifying experience, skill development and flexible action planning. Scenarios and model answers in this pack are original teaching examples.

lessons.title: What is a career? My journey so far
lessons.big_question: How is a career bigger than one job?
lessons.objective: I can explain what a job and a career are and say one thing I might like to do in the future.
success: I can sort jobs and other experiences.
I can explain that a career develops over time.
I can name a possibility or something I want to find out.

vocabulary.meaning: A particular work role a person does.
A journey through learning, work and life experiences.
Something a person does, learns or takes part in.
Something a person might want to achieve or explore.

slides.title: What is a career? My journey so far
body: How is a career bigger than one job?
I can explain what a job and a career are and say one thing I might like to do in the future.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct BUILD Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: A baker is a job. Is a college course a job too?
Can learning count in a career journey?
slides.prompt: Choose: job / learning / not sure.
slides.answer: A college course is learning. Learning can be part of a career journey.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: A journey has many parts
body: A job is one particular work role.
A career can include learning, different jobs, breaks and changes.
An idea for the future is a possibility, not a promise.
slides.prompt: Does a career have to stay the same?
slides.answer: No. New experience, learning and circumstances can change a career.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 8 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Meet Casey — a fictional journey
body: Past: Casey tried drawing maps in class.
Now: Casey practises using a design program.
Next possibility: find out how people design signs.
slides.prompt: Name one experience and one possible next step.
slides.answer: Drawing maps is an experience. Asking about sign design is a possible next step; it is not a guaranteed job.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Sort together
body: Cards: electrician; college course; club organiser.
Use job / learning or activity / other life role.
Some cards could fit more than one heading.
slides.prompt: Where might club organiser go? Explain.
slides.answer: It could be an unpaid activity or a life role; if paid, it could be a job. The card does not say, so explain the uncertainty.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: One job or a whole journey?
body: A: “A career means one job forever.”
B: “A career includes experiences and may change.”
slides.prompt: Choose the clearer explanation.
slides.answer: B. One job can be part of a wider career.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Sort six cards: Write a heading beside each card; explain one choice.
2. Make a three-step journey: Use Casey or a safe example of your own.
3. Record a starting point: Choose clear idea / several ideas / not sure yet, then finish one sentence.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 12 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can sort jobs and other experiences.
I can explain that a career develops over time.
I can name a possibility or something I want to find out.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when the pupil distinguishes job from career and records one possibility or enquiry. The aspiration itself is not marked.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Baseline career-readiness response; aspiration card.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Explain job and career using Casey or another example.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: A job is a particular work role; a career is a developing journey that can include learning and several roles.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: What is a career? My journey so far — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Sort six cards
tasks.prompt: Write a heading beside each card; explain one choice.
items: Electrician
College course
Café worker
Learning a design program
Friend
Club organiser
tasks.answer: Electrician and café worker: jobs. College course and design learning: learning/activity. Friend: life role. Club organiser: activity/role; accept job only if pupil explains that paid status is unknown.

tasks.heading: 2. Make a three-step journey
tasks.prompt: Use Casey or a safe example of your own.
items: Past: something learned or tried.
Now: an activity or learning step.
Possible future: something to explore; “not sure yet” is allowed.
tasks.answer: Casey: drew maps → practises a design program → asks about sign design. A coherent personal or fictional sequence is acceptable.

tasks.heading: 3. Record a starting point
tasks.prompt: Choose clear idea / several ideas / not sure yet, then finish one sentence.
items: I might explore… because…
One question I want to ask is…
tasks.answer: Example: Casey has several ideas and might explore design because map drawing was enjoyable. Question: What tasks do sign designers do?

worksheet.exit_question: Explain job and career using Casey or another example.
worksheet.exit_answer: A job is a particular work role; a career is a developing journey that can include learning and several roles.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: Drawing maps is an experience. Asking about sign design is a possible next step; it is not a guaranteed job. It could be an unpaid activity or a life role; if paid, it could be a job. The card does not say, so explain the uncertainty.
misconceptions: A career means one job forever → show different steps and the possibility of change.
Only paid work counts → learning and activities can also shape a career.
Everyone must choose now → uncertainty can lead to a useful question.
teacher.support: Use three cards first, read labels aloud and point to past/now/possible future. Scribe the learner’s words. Supply Casey so no personal history is needed.
teacher.stretch: Explain why the club-organiser card has more than one possible heading and what information would settle it.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when the pupil distinguishes job from career and records one possibility or enquiry. The aspiration itself is not marked.

resources.title: Job, experience and role cards
resources.instructions: Cut or point. Sort under job / learning or activity / other life role. Overlap needs a reason.
items: Electrician — installs or repairs electrical systems.
Café worker — prepares or serves items as part of a work role.
College course — a planned programme of learning.
Learning a design program — practising a new tool.
Friend — a relationship with another person.
Club organiser — organises meetings; the card does not state whether the role is paid.
answers: Jobs: electrician, café worker.
Learning/activity: course, learning a program.
Life role: friend. Club organiser may overlap; the missing paid-status detail prevents a single required placement.

resources.title: Casey’s journey card
resources.instructions: This is a fictional learning example, not a real career prediction.
items: Past: Casey drew maps for a classroom display and enjoyed choosing symbols.
Now: Casey practises making a clear sign in a design program.
Future: Casey is curious about signs and maps but has not chosen a job.
Casey could ask: “What does someone who designs public signs actually do?”
answers: A useful journey includes learning and change.
Curiosity is enough for a starting point; uncertainty is a valid baseline.

lessons.title: My strengths
lessons.big_question: How can an example show a strength?
lessons.objective: I can name at least three strengths and give an example of one.
success: I can name three strengths.
I can match an action to a strength.
I can give one example that supports a strength.

vocabulary.meaning: Something a person does well or is developing confidence in.
An ability learned and practised.
A specific example that supports a claim.
Follows through on an agreed task or communicates when plans change.

slides.title: My strengths
body: How can an example show a strength?
I can name at least three strengths and give an example of one.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct BUILD Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: Is “I am good at everything” useful evidence?
What could a person show instead?
slides.prompt: Choose: a big claim / a clear example.
slides.answer: A clear example shows what the person actually did.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Strength + example
body: A strength is a useful quality or capability.
A skill can be learned and practised; strengths can develop too.
An example helps us see what someone did.
slides.prompt: Which is clearer: “organised” or “made a checklist before the task”?
slides.answer: The checklist describes an action. Link it to organisation.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 8 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Alex finishes an agreed job
body: Alex agreed to label the group’s three trays.
Alex labelled all three and told the group they were ready.
slides.prompt: Which strength is supported?
slides.answer: Reliability: Alex completed the agreed action and communicated. This one event does not prove Alex is always reliable.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Find the clue
body: Sam checked a recipe after noticing a missing step.
Taylor used a prompt card, asked a question and continued.
slides.prompt: Choose a strength for each and point to its clue.
slides.answer: Sam: problem-solving/carefulness, shown by checking the recipe. Taylor: persistence, shown by using support and continuing.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: Support and strengths
body: A: “Using help means you have no strengths.”
B: “Using the right help can show a useful strategy.”
slides.prompt: Which statement is fairer?
slides.answer: B. Asking a useful question or using a prompt can help someone demonstrate a skill.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Choose three strengths: Choose for yourself or the fictional learner Rowan.
2. Match action to strength: Choose a strength and underline the action that supports it.
3. Prove one strength: Write, draw or explain an example. Mark it personal example or fictional case.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 12 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can name three strengths.
I can match an action to a strength.
I can give one example that supports a strength.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when three strengths are identified and at least one is supported by a specific action. Case analysis is labelled separately from personal portfolio evidence.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Strengths profile with one example.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Name three strengths and give an example for one.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: For Rowan: organised, careful, persistent. Organisation is supported by sorting the project cards.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: My strengths — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Choose three strengths
tasks.prompt: Choose for yourself or the fictional learner Rowan.
items: Strength bank: reliable, organised, creative, patient, practical, helpful, careful, persistent.
Rowan sorted project cards, checked every label and tried a second layout after the first did not fit.
tasks.answer: Rowan: organised, careful and persistent. Own choices are accepted without public disclosure; avoid inventing evidence.

tasks.heading: 2. Match action to strength
tasks.prompt: Choose a strength and underline the action that supports it.
items: Alex labelled the three trays they agreed to prepare.
Sam checked the recipe when a step seemed missing.
Taylor used a prompt card and continued after difficulty.
tasks.answer: Alex: reliability. Sam: carefulness/problem-solving. Taylor: persistence/using support. Accept other strengths if linked to the stated action.

tasks.heading: 3. Prove one strength
tasks.prompt: Write, draw or explain an example. Mark it personal example or fictional case.
items: The strength is…
The person did…
This supports the strength because…
tasks.answer: Rowan showed organisation by sorting project cards before arranging them. “Rowan is amazing” is too vague.

worksheet.exit_question: Name three strengths and give an example for one.
worksheet.exit_answer: For Rowan: organised, careful, persistent. Organisation is supported by sorting the project cards.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: Reliability: Alex completed the agreed action and communicated. This one event does not prove Alex is always reliable. Sam: problem-solving/carefulness, shown by checking the recipe. Taylor: persistence, shown by using support and continuing.
misconceptions: Strengths are fixed → practice and support can develop them.
Being quiet means poor communication → communication has many forms.
Evidence must be impressive → a small accurate example is useful.
teacher.support: Reduce the bank to organised/careful/persistent. Highlight one action at a time. Accept pointing plus a scribed explanation.
teacher.stretch: Find two strengths in one action and explain which is better supported. Avoid claiming an action proves a permanent personality trait.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when three strengths are identified and at least one is supported by a specific action. Case analysis is labelled separately from personal portfolio evidence.

resources.title: Strength bank
resources.instructions: Use words or point; no strength belongs to one kind of person.
items: Reliable — follows through or communicates a change.
Organised — keeps track of tasks or materials.
Creative — develops ideas or tries a new approach.
Patient — gives a task or person time.
Practical — uses hands-on methods to make or solve.
Helpful — offers useful support without taking over.
Careful — checks detail or safe steps.
Persistent — tries again or uses support after difficulty.
answers: A person may show several strengths in one activity.
Asking for support is compatible with these strengths.

resources.title: Rowan’s display project
resources.instructions: Use this complete fictional case if you prefer not to write about yourself.
items: Rowan sorted six project cards into two groups.
Rowan checked that each label matched its card.
The first layout did not fit the display space.
Rowan used the teacher’s grid and rearranged the cards successfully.
answers: Organised: sorted cards.
Careful: checked labels.
Persistent/problem-solving: used the grid and rearranged.

lessons.title: My interests and working preferences
lessons.big_question: What do I enjoy, and what helps me work?
lessons.objective: I can identify things I enjoy and say whether I prefer working indoors/outdoors, with people/things, or active/quiet tasks.
success: I can identify three interests or curiosities.
I can make two preference choices, including both or unsure.
I can explain a choice without treating it as a fixed rule.

vocabulary.meaning: An activity or topic a person enjoys or wants to explore.
A way of working someone tends to choose.
Something about a place or task, such as noise or routine.
Find out more before deciding.

slides.title: My interests and working preferences
body: What do I enjoy, and what helps me work?
I can identify things I enjoy and say whether I prefer working indoors/outdoors, with people/things, or active/quiet tasks.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct BUILD Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: Does enjoying drawing mean someone already has every design skill?
Can a preference change with experience?
slides.prompt: Answer yes / no / not sure, then explain one.
slides.answer: Enjoyment and skill differ. Preferences can change after experience.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Interests are clues
body: Interest: something you enjoy or are curious about.
Preference: a way of working that may help you.
You may choose both, a mix or not sure yet.
slides.prompt: Is an interest the same as a guaranteed career?
slides.answer: No. It suggests a question to explore; it does not predict a job.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 8 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Sam’s profile — use only the clues
body: Sam enjoys drawing maps and showing a classmate how a program works.
Noise makes concentrating harder; a written task list helps.
Sam is happy using a computer for part of a lesson.
slides.prompt: Name one interest, one preference and one unknown.
slides.answer: Interest: maps/digital tasks/helping. Preference: calmer setting/clear written steps. Unknown: indoors or outdoors; the case does not say.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Choices can be a mix
body: Indoors / outdoors / both / unsure.
With people / independently / both / unsure.
Steady routine / variety / both / unsure.
slides.prompt: Could a person prefer people and a calmer place?
slides.answer: Yes. These are separate preferences; social contact does not have to mean a noisy setting.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: A clue is not a rule
body: A: “Sam plays games, so Sam must become a game designer.”
B: “Sam could explore digital tasks and see which parts are enjoyable.”
slides.prompt: Choose the better statement.
slides.answer: B. Playing and creating games involve different tasks; investigate before assuming fit.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Select interests: Choose three for yourself or Sam. Add a curiosity if you are unsure.
2. Choose how to work: For each pair write left / right / mix / unsure. Explain two choices.
3. Make an exploration card: Link an interest or preference to something worth finding out.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 12 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can identify three interests or curiosities.
I can make two preference choices, including both or unsure.
I can explain a choice without treating it as a fixed rule.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when the pupil records interests and makes two reasoned preference choices or specific enquiries. No career match is treated as compulsory.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Interest/preference record.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Give two preference choices and one reason, or explain what would help you decide.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: Example for Sam: calmer space because noise makes concentrating harder; written steps because they help Sam begin.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: My interests and working preferences — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Select interests
tasks.prompt: Choose three for yourself or Sam. Add a curiosity if you are unsure.
items: Making; drawing; digital tools; cooking; sport; nature; helping; fixing; music; organising.
Sam: draws maps, explains a program and enjoys solving small software problems.
tasks.answer: Sam might choose drawing, digital tools and helping/problem-solving. There is no required personal combination.

tasks.heading: 2. Choose how to work
tasks.prompt: For each pair write left / right / mix / unsure. Explain two choices.
items: Indoors or outdoors.
With people or independently.
Hands-on tasks or desk/computer tasks.
Routine or variety.
Calmer or busier setting.
Predictable hours or changing hours.
tasks.answer: Sam supports calmer setting and clear steps; some digital/people tasks are liked. Other pairs remain unsure. Do not infer that clear instructions require an unchanging routine.

tasks.heading: 3. Make an exploration card
tasks.prompt: Link an interest or preference to something worth finding out.
items: I might explore… because…
I still need to know…
tasks.answer: Sam might explore creating digital maps because of drawing and program interests. Question: Which tasks involve making maps, and how much teamwork is involved?

worksheet.exit_question: Give two preference choices and one reason, or explain what would help you decide.
worksheet.exit_answer: Example for Sam: calmer space because noise makes concentrating harder; written steps because they help Sam begin.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: Interest: maps/digital tasks/helping. Preference: calmer setting/clear written steps. Unknown: indoors or outdoors; the case does not say. Yes. These are separate preferences; social contact does not have to mean a noisy setting.
misconceptions: An interest is a qualification → enjoyment and skill are different.
Preference is permanent → revise after trying something.
Quiet work means working alone → noise level and social contact are different.
teacher.support: Use three preference pairs initially and a both/unsure card. Allow a fictional profile with evidence rather than requiring a personal choice.
teacher.stretch: Name a preference we cannot infer about Sam and suggest a short, low-pressure activity that could reveal more.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when the pupil records interests and makes two reasoned preference choices or specific enquiries. No career match is treated as compulsory.

resources.title: Preference choice cards
resources.instructions: Use one pair at a time. Both and not sure yet are valid.
items: Indoors / outdoors / mix / unsure.
Working with people / independently / mix / unsure.
Hands-on / desk and computer / mix / unsure.
Routine / variety / mix / unsure.
Calmer / busier / mix / unsure.
Predictable hours / changing hours / mix / unsure.
answers: No preference is morally better.
Clear instructions and a supportive environment can help across many settings.
A job can include both sides of a pair.

resources.title: Sam’s interests case
items: Sam likes drawing maps and solving small problems in a design program.
Sam explained one program tool to a classmate and enjoyed helping.
A noisy room makes concentration harder. Written steps help Sam begin.
Sam is happy at a computer for part of a lesson.
No information is given about outdoor work, shifts, pay or preferred group size.
answers: Interests: drawing/maps, digital tasks, helping, problem-solving.
Supported preferences: quieter conditions; written instructions.
Do not infer shift pattern, pay priorities or that all solo work is preferred.

lessons.title: Values, belonging and the workplace
lessons.big_question: What helps people feel respected and able to take part?
lessons.objective: I can identify two things that would help me feel comfortable and respected at work.
success: I can recognise respectful treatment.
I can name two conditions that help someone work.
I can explain why those conditions matter.

vocabulary.meaning: Something a person considers important.
Feeling accepted and able to take part.
Treating people with care and listening seriously.
Help or a change that enables someone to participate.

slides.title: Values, belonging and the workplace
body: What helps people feel respected and able to take part?
I can identify two things that would help me feel comfortable and respected at work.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct BUILD Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: Which helps learning: questions welcomed or questions mocked?
Name one useful way to give feedback.
slides.prompt: Choose and explain.
slides.answer: Welcoming questions supports learning. Calm, specific feedback helps someone understand a next step.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Respect is for everyone
body: Safety, fair treatment and dignity are expectations for everyone.
People can prefer different tasks, routines and settings.
Support helps participation; needing it is not a failure.
slides.prompt: Should a pupil rank safety as unimportant to get a preferred task?
slides.answer: No. Compare preferences without treating safety, dignity or fairness as things to give away.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 8 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Alex’s two workplaces
body: Alex likes practical tasks, clear steps and calm feedback.
Place A: induction, written steps and questions welcomed.
Place B: no explanation; mistakes mocked in front of others.
slides.prompt: Which place supports Alex? What needs changing in B?
slides.answer: A supports learning. B needs clear induction and respectful private feedback; mockery is not simply a different preference.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Turn a value into an action
body: Value: respect → listen and use a calm tone.
Value: clarity → show the first step and who can help.
Value: inclusion → offer a way for each person to join in.
slides.prompt: What might “support” look like during a new task?
slides.answer: A demonstration, written steps, a named person for questions, or a planned check-in; choose a response matching the task.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: Preference or shared expectation?
body: A: working outside for part of the day.
B: not being mocked for asking a question.
C: some variety in tasks.
slides.prompt: Which should apply to everyone?
slides.answer: B. A and C can be individual preferences. Respect and safety are not optional trade-offs.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Recognise useful conditions: Mark each as supportive / needs changing.
2. Compare Alex’s workplaces: Use the resource card. Name two useful conditions and one repair.
3. Complete a workplace-values card: Use yourself or Alex. Name two helpful conditions and give reasons.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 12 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can recognise respectful treatment.
I can name two conditions that help someone work.
I can explain why those conditions matter.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when two helpful conditions are named and linked to participation. Check that disrespect is identified as a problem, not ranked as a tolerable preference.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Workplace-values card.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Name two helpful workplace conditions and explain one.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: Alex benefits from written steps and calm feedback; written steps make the next action clearer.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: Values, belonging and the workplace — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Recognise useful conditions
tasks.prompt: Mark each as supportive / needs changing.
items: A supervisor demonstrates a new tool safely.
People mock a worker who asks a question.
The task list shows who can help.
Feedback names the next step calmly.
tasks.answer: Supportive: safe demonstration, named help, calm feedback. Mocking questions needs changing.

tasks.heading: 2. Compare Alex’s workplaces
tasks.prompt: Use the resource card. Name two useful conditions and one repair.
items: Place A helps Alex because…
A second helpful condition is…
Place B should change…
tasks.answer: A: written steps, calm feedback, named helper/induction. B should replace public mockery with respectful feedback and teach the task.

tasks.heading: 3. Complete a workplace-values card
tasks.prompt: Use yourself or Alex. Name two helpful conditions and give reasons.
items: Condition 1… helps because…
Condition 2… helps because…
Respect, safety and fair treatment remain expectations for everyone.
tasks.answer: Alex: clear steps help starting accurately; calm feedback helps understanding mistakes and next steps. Do not ask pupils to tolerate disrespect to obtain a preferred role.

worksheet.exit_question: Name two helpful workplace conditions and explain one.
worksheet.exit_answer: Alex benefits from written steps and calm feedback; written steps make the next action clearer.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: A supports learning. B needs clear induction and respectful private feedback; mockery is not simply a different preference. A demonstration, written steps, a named person for questions, or a planned check-in; choose a response matching the task.
misconceptions: Respect is just a preference → it is an expectation for everyone.
Belonging means everyone is the same → different people can participate.
Support means inability → well-chosen support enables skills to be shown.
teacher.support: Start with supportive/needs-changing cards. Offer two conditions to choose between and a “helps because” stem. Use Alex throughout.
teacher.stretch: Suggest two different ways to provide clear instructions without assuming every learner needs the same support.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when two helpful conditions are named and linked to participation. Check that disrespect is identified as a problem, not ranked as a tolerable preference.

resources.title: Alex’s workplace comparison
resources.instructions: Fictional places. Discuss treatment using the words on the card; no personal experience is required.
items: Alex enjoys practical work and works well with clear instructions and calm feedback.
Place A shows the task, gives written steps, identifies a helper and welcomes questions.
Place B says “You should know”, gives no clear instructions and mocks questions or mistakes.
Alex has not yet tried either place. The comparison is based only on the information given.
answers: A gives stronger support for learning.
B’s mockery is a problem to challenge, not an acceptable price for practical work.
We cannot judge pay, travel or every condition because those details are absent.

resources.title: Conditions and actions cards
resources.instructions: Match a condition to an action. More than one action can support the same condition.
items: Clear instructions — show the task and provide a short step list.
Support — name a person who can answer a question.
Respect — give feedback calmly and avoid humiliation.
Inclusion — make a contribution possible in different ways.
Routine — explain the day’s sequence in advance where possible.
Variety — include different task types when appropriate.
answers: Clear instructions, support, respect and inclusion can help participation.
Routine and variety are preferences that vary by person; discuss what helps the particular learner.

lessons.title: Skills I already use
lessons.big_question: How can an everyday activity show a work skill?
lessons.objective: I can match at least three things I already do to work skills such as communication, teamwork, organising or problem-solving.
success: I can match three actions to skills.
I can point to evidence for a skill.
I can explain how one skill could help elsewhere.

vocabulary.meaning: Useful in more than one task or place.
Sharing and understanding information.
Contributing with others to a shared task.
Planning and keeping track of steps or materials.

slides.title: Skills I already use
body: How can an everyday activity show a work skill?
I can match at least three things I already do to work skills such as communication, teamwork, organising or problem-solving.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct BUILD Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: A person explains a game’s rules clearly. Which skill is shown?
Can that skill help outside the game?
slides.prompt: Choose communication / guesswork.
slides.answer: Communication. Clear explanations can also help in school projects or a work task.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Activity → skill → evidence
body: Activity: the task that happened.
Skill: the useful ability within the task.
Evidence: what the person actually did.
slides.prompt: Is “I went to ICT” enough to show digital skill?
slides.answer: No. Say what the person did, such as naming and saving a file in the right folder.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 8 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Sam’s school display task
body: Sam checked the materials list and shared jobs.
Sam explained the plan and asked staff about a missing item.
Sam made a paper title; no digital tool is mentioned.
slides.prompt: Which skills can we see?
slides.answer: Organisation, teamwork, communication and problem-solving. A paper title alone does not show digital-tool use.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Find three links
body: Checked the list → organisation.
Shared jobs → teamwork.
Explained the plan → communication.
slides.prompt: What exact action supports each link?
slides.answer: The action on each card supplies the evidence. Accept an additional skill only if the action supports it.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: Can we claim it?
body: A: “Sam used software for the title.”
B: “Sam planned the materials.”
slides.prompt: Which claim is supported by the case?
slides.answer: B. The title was on paper; do not invent a digital action.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Match the actions: Match each action to a skill from the bank.
2. Make three evidence strips: Use your own safe examples or Sam. Mark which you use.
3. Transfer one skill: Choose one skill and explain another task where it could help.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 12 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can match three actions to skills.
I can point to evidence for a skill.
I can explain how one skill could help elsewhere.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when three activity-to-skill links are made, at least one with a specific explanation. Fictional examples demonstrate analysis, not the learner’s work history.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Transferable-skills evidence strip.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Give one activity, one skill and the action that links them.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: During the display task Sam checked the materials list. This shows organisation because Sam prepared resources before starting.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: Skills I already use — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Match the actions
tasks.prompt: Match each action to a skill from the bank.
items: Explained the display plan clearly.
Shared the measuring and arranging jobs.
Checked the list before starting.
Asked staff about a safe replacement for a missing item.
tasks.answer: Communication; teamwork; organisation; problem-solving. More than one match can be accepted with a reason.

tasks.heading: 2. Make three evidence strips
tasks.prompt: Use your own safe examples or Sam. Mark which you use.
items: Action 1… shows…
Action 2… shows…
Action 3… shows…
tasks.answer: Sam checked materials, shared jobs and explained the plan: organisation, teamwork, communication. Personal evidence must be authentic and specific.

tasks.heading: 3. Transfer one skill
tasks.prompt: Choose one skill and explain another task where it could help.
items: The skill is…
It could help in… because…
tasks.answer: Clear communication could help explaining a practical task to a colleague. Organisation could help checking stock. Do not claim that one example proves full job competence.

worksheet.exit_question: Give one activity, one skill and the action that links them.
worksheet.exit_answer: During the display task Sam checked the materials list. This shows organisation because Sam prepared resources before starting.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: Organisation, teamwork, communication and problem-solving. A paper title alone does not show digital-tool use. The action on each card supplies the evidence. Accept an additional skill only if the action supports it.
misconceptions: No paid job means no useful skills → school tasks can show skills.
A subject name proves a skill → identify the action.
Missing evidence means no ability → it means we need more information.
teacher.support: Use communication/teamwork/organisation first. Point to an action and select one of two skill cards. Record three short oral strips if writing is a barrier.
teacher.stretch: Explain how the same action can show two skills while distinguishing what is stated from what is assumed.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when three activity-to-skill links are made, at least one with a specific explanation. Fictional examples demonstrate analysis, not the learner’s work history.

resources.title: Sam’s display-project evidence
resources.instructions: Fictional case. Read exactly what happened before choosing a skill.
items: Sam checked the list of card, tape and labels before starting.
Sam agreed with a classmate who would measure and who would arrange the cards.
Sam explained the agreed layout to the group.
One item was missing. Sam asked staff about a safe alternative.
Sam wrote the title on paper. The case does not describe a digital tool.
answers: Organisation: checked list. Teamwork: agreed shared jobs.
Communication: explained layout. Problem-solving: recognised missing item and asked about an alternative.
Digital evidence is absent; unknown is not evidence of inability.

resources.title: Five skill cards
resources.instructions: Keep the skill separate from the activity.
items: Communication — explain, listen, ask or use an agreed communication aid.
Teamwork — share roles and contribute to a joint aim.
Problem-solving — notice a problem and try a suitable response.
Organisation — plan steps and keep track of resources.
Digital — use a device or software for a purposeful task.
answers: One activity can demonstrate several skills.
Digital skill needs a stated digital action, not an assumption based on the task.

lessons.title: Jobs for people like me — challenging stereotypes
lessons.big_question: What should we use to judge whether a job is worth exploring?
lessons.objective: I can identify a stereotype about work and explain that people should be judged by skills and interests.
success: I can recognise an unfair group assumption.
I can name real tasks or skills relevant to a role.
I can explain why identity alone does not decide suitability.

vocabulary.meaning: A fixed assumption about a group of people.
Something genuinely needed for a particular role or task.
How a person’s skills, interests and needs relate to a task.
Information that supports a judgement.

slides.title: Challenging career stereotypes
body: What should we use to judge whether a job is worth exploring?
I can identify a stereotype about work and explain that people should be judged by skills and interests.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct BUILD Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: Which tells us more: a person’s gender or what they can do?
A task needs safe tool use. Is that linked to the work?
slides.prompt: Choose evidence / assumption.
slides.answer: Relevant actions and genuine task requirements provide evidence. Gender does not show tool competence.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: Ask about the work
body: A stereotype guesses from group identity.
A fairer judgement uses relevant skills, interests and task evidence.
Training and access needs must be explored individually.
slides.prompt: Does challenging stereotypes mean no training is needed?
slides.answer: No. Real task requirements still matter; group assumptions do not establish competence.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 8 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Meet Noor — fictional trainee technician
body: Noor enjoys finding faults and follows a checking sequence.
Noor uses a wheelchair and a bench arranged for access.
A comment says: “Disabled people cannot do technical work.”
slides.prompt: What is the assumption? What evidence should we use?
slides.answer: The comment assumes disability rules out all technical work. Check Noor’s actual problem-solving, training, task requirements and access arrangements.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Requirement or assumption?
body: “This task needs careful checking.”
“Only men can repair things.”
“This task needs following a safe sequence.”
slides.prompt: Which statement is the stereotype?
slides.answer: “Only men can repair things.” The other two describe task-related requirements, although exact requirements vary by role.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: Choose a fairer sentence
body: A: “Anyone can do any job without training.”
B: “Explore the person’s skills, interests, requirements and support.”
slides.prompt: Which avoids both a stereotype and an unrealistic promise?
slides.answer: B. Individual evidence and actual requirements matter.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Sort four statements: Write requirement / stereotype and explain one.
2. Challenge the comment: Use Noor’s card. Replace the group assumption with evidence.
3. Make an exploration card: Choose Noor or another supplied fictional example.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 12 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can recognise an unfair group assumption.
I can name real tasks or skills relevant to a role.
I can explain why identity alone does not decide suitability.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Secure when the pupil identifies one group assumption and replaces it with relevant skill/task evidence. Never assess a learner’s identity or personal disclosure.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Stereotype-challenge response / role-model card.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Challenge one career stereotype with a reason.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: “Only men can use tools” is a stereotype. We should look at safe skills, training and the actual task, not gender.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: Jobs for people like me — challenging stereotypes — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Sort four statements
tasks.prompt: Write requirement / stereotype and explain one.
items: A repair task needs careful checking.
Only men can work with tools.
A care task needs safe, respectful communication.
Quiet people cannot contribute to a team.
tasks.answer: Requirements: checking; safe respectful communication. Stereotypes: only men; quiet people. Quiet workers may contribute in several ways.

tasks.heading: 2. Challenge the comment
tasks.prompt: Use Noor’s card. Replace the group assumption with evidence.
items: The assumption says…
The evidence shows…
We should check…
tasks.answer: Assumption: disability excludes technical work. Evidence: fault-finding and a checking sequence. Check task competence, training and access requirements individually.

tasks.heading: 3. Make an exploration card
tasks.prompt: Choose Noor or another supplied fictional example.
items: Role or area worth exploring…
Two relevant skills or tasks…
One question about learning or access…
tasks.answer: Noor: technical repair; systematic checking and problem-solving; ask which training and workstation arrangements the role involves. Accept other evidence-based examples.

worksheet.exit_question: Challenge one career stereotype with a reason.
worksheet.exit_answer: “Only men can use tools” is a stereotype. We should look at safe skills, training and the actual task, not gender.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: The comment assumes disability rules out all technical work. Check Noor’s actual problem-solving, training, task requirements and access arrangements. “Only men can repair things.” The other two describe task-related requirements, although exact requirements vary by role.
misconceptions: Any opinion is a stereotype → identify the group assumption.
Rejecting stereotypes means no requirements → training and safe competence still matter.
Support guarantees every role will fit → investigate individual access and tasks without promising an outcome.
teacher.support: Read one short statement at a time. Provide requirement/assumption cards and use Noor or Elliot without asking pupils to reveal identity or experience.
teacher.stretch: Explain how an assumption may create an access barrier, and suggest a question that would replace guessing with evidence.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Secure when the pupil identifies one group assumption and replaces it with relevant skill/task evidence. Never assess a learner’s identity or personal disclosure.

resources.title: Fictional career examples
resources.instructions: These invented people are learning cases, not real biographies or guarantees of employment.
items: Noor: trainee technician; enjoys fault-finding, practises safe checks, uses a wheelchair and an accessible bench. A tutor checks each new task.
Elliot: interested in care work; communicates calmly and checks whether another person wants help. Elliot is male.
Jules: quiet during whole-class talk; contributes written plans and listens carefully in a small project team.
For all three, the exact job, training and access needs still need investigation.
answers: Noor challenges an assumption that disability rules out technical work.
Elliot challenges a gender assumption about care.
Jules challenges the assumption that only loud speakers can contribute to teams.

resources.title: Statement sort
resources.instructions: Classify the words, not the worth of any person.
items: A repair task needs careful checking.
Only men can work with tools.
A care task needs safe, respectful communication.
Quiet people cannot contribute to a team.
Some tasks require specific training before independent work.
A person’s background tells us whether they will be reliable.
answers: Task-related requirements: checking, safe communication, relevant training.
Stereotypes: only men, quiet people cannot, background predicts reliability.
Some group assumptions can also create real access barriers; the categories are not a denial of harm.

lessons.title: My vocational profile
lessons.big_question: How can I bring my evidence together and choose a next question?
lessons.objective: I can create a one-page profile showing what I am good at, what I like and jobs I want to explore.
success: I can collect strengths, interests and useful conditions.
I can link an area to evidence in a profile.
I can choose one small next action.

vocabulary.meaning: A short record of strengths, interests, preferences and possible next steps.
Open to change after new experience or information.
A specific next step to work towards.
Look again and update using evidence.

slides.title: My vocational profile
body: How can I bring my evidence together and choose a next question?
I can create a one-page profile showing what I am good at, what I like and jobs I want to explore.
Use your own safe examples or the fictional case. Share only what you choose.
slides.notes: Adapted from the supplied lesson and the distinct BUILD Autumn 1 weekly outcome. Original activities and fully supplied paper cases are included.

slides.title: Start here
body: Find one strength, one interest and one useful condition in your earlier work.
No earlier sheets? Use Sam’s complete profile card.
slides.prompt: Which is supported by an example?
slides.answer: An action such as checking ingredients supports organisation; an unsupported label needs more evidence.
slides.notes: Arrival and baseline: 5 minutes. Give thinking time before inviting voluntary responses.

slides.title: A profile is a starting point
body: Record strengths and the actions that support them.
Add interests, ways of working and questions.
Choose areas to explore; you do not need a final job today.
slides.prompt: Can a profile change next term?
slides.answer: Yes. New tasks, support, experience and information can change it.
slides.notes: Explicit teaching: 8 minutes shared with the following model slide.

slides.title: Sam brings evidence together
body: Sam plans ingredients, follows steps and adjusts a model after feedback.
Sam likes practical making and seeing a finished result.
Written steps and time to ask a question help Sam.
slides.prompt: Suggest an area and a reason, without deciding Sam’s future.
slides.answer: Catering or practical design/maintenance could be explored because of planning and making interests. The profile does not establish entry requirements or guarantee fit.
slides.notes: Read the complete accompanying case card if pupils need all details. Think aloud using evidence; do not infer missing facts.

slides.title: Turn an area into a next step
body: Area: practical food work.
Question: which tasks are part of a typical day?
Action: ask the teacher to help compare two role descriptions next lesson.
slides.prompt: What makes that action manageable?
slides.answer: It says what to do, who can help and when. It gathers information rather than requiring a final choice.
slides.notes: Guided practice: 10 minutes shared with the next check. Pupil resources contain the full text.

slides.title: Check the profile
body: A: “Good at everything; will definitely be a chef.”
B: “Plans ingredients; could explore food roles; needs to check typical tasks.”
slides.prompt: Which profile uses evidence and leaves a useful question?
slides.answer: B. A is vague and makes an unsupported promise.
slides.notes: Check the reason as well as the selected answer. Accept justified alternatives where indicated.

slides.title: Your three tasks
body: 1. Gather the strongest evidence: Use earlier sheets or Sam’s full card.
2. Create the profile: Write or draw a one-page profile using the headings below.
3. Set one first target: Choose a small action with help and a review point.
slides.prompt: Use the worksheet and resource cards. Work one task at a time.
slides.notes: Application: 12 minutes including the improve slide. Offer pointing, speaking, drawing, typing or scribing.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: I can collect strengths, interests and useful conditions.
I can link an area to evidence in a profile.
I can choose one small next action.
slides.prompt: Choose one part to make clearer. Which detail supports your answer?
slides.answer: Summative review: three strengths, one evidence example, interests, useful conditions, one or more justified areas and a specific next action. Record secure/developing/next step for each; avoid a score for career prestige.
slides.notes: Check understanding, reasoning and independence. Never grade the prestige of an aspiration or willingness to share personal information.

slides.title: Save your evidence
body: Completed vocational profile and first career target.
Mark the work: my own example / fictional case analysis.
Keep one question open for your next lesson.
slides.prompt: Which piece shows today’s learning?
slides.notes: Final reflection, portfolio filing and exit share 5 minutes. Allow a calm reset; do not require public reading of a profile.

slides.title: Exit check
body: Name one area to explore, an evidence-based reason and a next step.
slides.prompt: Answer using words, pointing, a sketch or a private adult conversation.
slides.answer: Sam could explore catering because planning ingredients was enjoyable; next lesson Sam can compare typical tasks with teacher support.
slides.notes: Collect a short independent response. No fixed career decision is required.

worksheet.title: My vocational profile — pupil record

tasks.heading: 1. Gather the strongest evidence
tasks.prompt: Use earlier sheets or Sam’s full card.
items: Three strengths, with one action as evidence.
Two interests and one transferable skill.
Two useful working conditions or supports.
tasks.answer: Sam: organised/practical/persistent; planned ingredients. Interests: making/food. Skill: organisation. Conditions: written steps, time for questions.

tasks.heading: 2. Create the profile
tasks.prompt: Write or draw a one-page profile using the headings below.
items: Good at / evidence.
Enjoys / works best with.
Two job areas to explore / reason for each.
tasks.answer: Sam could explore catering and practical design/maintenance; both link to making, planning and visible results. Other areas are accepted if evidence supports the link. A job title is not required.

tasks.heading: 3. Set one first target
tasks.prompt: Choose a small action with help and a review point.
items: I will find out…
I can ask/use…
I will check this by…
tasks.answer: Sam will ask the teacher next Careers lesson to compare typical tasks in two practical roles, then review which sounds worth investigating.

worksheet.exit_question: Name one area to explore, an evidence-based reason and a next step.
worksheet.exit_answer: Sam could explore catering because planning ingredients was enjoyable; next lesson Sam can compare typical tasks with teacher support.

preparation: Print the worksheet and complete resource cards; prepare cut cards only where used.
Have the previous portfolio sheet available, plus the supplied fictional case for absent pupils or those choosing privacy.
Prepare the learner’s established reading, communication and regulation supports.

timing.activity: Arrival and retrieval; low-stakes response
I Do: explain and model using the supplied case
We Do: guided task and reasoning check
You Do: three worksheet tasks, feedback and improvement
Reflection, file evidence, exit check and calm reset

teacher.modelling: Catering or practical design/maintenance could be explored because of planning and making interests. The profile does not establish entry requirements or guarantee fit. It says what to do, who can help and when. It gathers information rather than requiring a final choice.
misconceptions: A profile is a final decision → it is revisable.
A support need rules out a whole area → investigate actual tasks and access.
A fictional profile proves personal skills → label case analysis honestly.
teacher.support: Use Sam’s completed evidence bank. Build one section at a time with drawings, pointing or scribing. Support naming two areas but accept one explained area as a next teaching step.
teacher.stretch: Choose a second plausible area and explain what new information might change the order of the shortlist.
teacher.fallback: No internet, photographs or personal history are needed. Read the supplied cards aloud and use the named fictional case. If a pupil needs a reset, resume with one card and record their explanation orally; complete remaining evidence later.
teacher.safeguarding: No required disclosure of family work, money, identity, disability, private experiences or future plans. Offer the same learning through fictional case analysis and label it accordingly. Do not invent personal evidence or promise access, a job or an adjustment. Follow school procedures if a concern is shared.
teacher.assessment: Summative review: three strengths, one evidence example, interests, useful conditions, one or more justified areas and a specific next action. Record secure/developing/next step for each; avoid a score for career prestige.

resources.title: Sam’s complete profile evidence
resources.instructions: Use if earlier work is missing or a fictional alternative is preferred.
items: Sam planned ingredients for a classroom food project using a checklist.
Sam followed clear steps to build a small card model.
After feedback, Sam changed the model so its parts fitted.
Sam enjoys practical making, food tasks and seeing a finished result.
Written steps and time to ask a question help Sam begin and continue.
Sam is curious about catering and practical design but has not investigated routes or real working days.
answers: Organisation: ingredient checklist. Practical skill: made a model. Persistence/problem-solving: revised it.
Possible areas require reasons; catering and practical design are examples, not the only correct answers.
Current unknowns include role tasks, learning routes and actual working conditions.

resources.title: Profile and first-target checklist
resources.instructions: Use to review the work, not to judge a pupil’s ambition.
items: Three strengths or positive capabilities.
One specific action supporting a strength.
Interests and a transferable skill.
Working conditions or support that help.
Two possible areas, with an evidence-based reason; one well-explained area is an acceptable supported starting point.
One question or small action, a helper/source and a review point.
Mark personal example or fictional case analysis.
answers: Secure learning shows accurate evidence and a sensible exploration step.
Personal aspirations can remain private. Fictional analysis meets the lesson’s reasoning objective, but is not a personal vocational assessment.
